sentences.en: What passing bells for those who die as cattle?
sentences.zh: 哪里的丧钟为这些像牛羊般死去的阵亡者而鸣？

sentences.en: Only the monstrous anger of the guns, only the stuttering rifle's rapid rattle can patter out their hasty orisons.
sentences.zh: 只有大炮那骇人的怒吼，只有机枪断断续续的急促爆裂声，在为他们仓促的祈祷伴奏。

sentences.en: The opening of Anthem for Doomed Youth by Wilfred Owen, famous war poet who died in action on the 4th of November, one week before the armistice brought peace at last
sentences.zh: 这是威尔弗雷德·欧文（Wilfred Owen）的《为毁灭的青年而作的挽歌》的开篇，这位著名的战争诗人于11月4日英勇牺牲，就在停战协定终于带来和平的一周前

sentences.en: to the Western Front.
sentences.zh: 在西线战场。

sentences.en: And it's kind of indicative, really, of the way that people in Britain have come to see
sentences.zh: 这其实在某种程度上暗示了英国人看待西线的方式，

sentences.en: the Western Front, from Wilfred Owen, it's a tracer line to the concept of lions led by donkeys,
sentences.zh: 从威尔弗雷德·欧文开始，这就与“驴子领导的狮子”这一概念一脉相承，

sentences.en: the joke in Blackadder of Haig making yet another gargantuan effort to move his drinks cabinet six inches closer to Berlin.
sentences.zh: 也就是《黑爵士》里的那个笑话：黑格又做出了一次极其庞大的努力，把他的酒柜向柏林方向挪动了六英寸。

sentences.en: And Dominic Sambra, you've actually written a book on the First World War, is that right?
sentences.zh: 多米尼克·桑布拉，你其实写过一本关于第一次世界大战的书，对吗？

sentences.en: A children's book.
sentences.zh: 一本童书。

sentences.en: A children's book, yeah.
sentences.zh: 一本童书，没错。

sentences.en: Yeah, but that's fine.
sentences.zh: 对，但那挺好的。

sentences.en: I mean, so you're kind of immersed in all this.
sentences.zh: 我的意思是，所以你基本上一直沉浸在这些之中。

sentences.en: I have been.
sentences.zh: 我确实一直如此。

sentences.en: This hasn't been published yet.
sentences.zh: 这本书还没出版呢。

sentences.en: It's been published just before Christmas.
sentences.zh: 它就在圣诞节前刚刚出版。

sentences.en: So I have – it's such a fascinating subject, Tom.
sentences.zh: 所以我——汤姆，这是一个多么迷人的主题。

sentences.en: And as you say, that – it's funny because I was thinking when you were doing that, when you were reading that poem, that we did that –
sentences.zh: 正如你所说，那——这很有趣，因为当你在做那个的时候，当你在读那首诗的时候，我在想，我们做了那个——

sentences.en: Did you like my Sambra voice?
sentences.zh: 你喜欢我的桑布拉模仿秀吗？

sentences.en: I thought it was beautiful.
sentences.zh: 我觉得太棒了。

sentences.en: I think if the history doesn't work out, and who knows if it will,
sentences.zh: 我想如果历史研究行不通的话——谁知道能不能行呢，

sentences.en: then a career as a reader of poetry, audiobooks –
sentences.zh: 那么去当个朗诵诗歌的播音员、有声书——

sentences.en: War poetry.
sentences.zh: 战争诗歌。

sentences.en: Yeah, war poetry.
sentences.zh: 对，战争诗歌。

sentences.en: I think you'd be great at that, Tom.
sentences.zh: 汤姆，我觉得你在这方面绝对能大显身手。

sentences.en: Thanks, all right.
sentences.zh: 谢谢，好吧。

sentences.en: Appreciate that.
sentences.zh: 非常感谢。

sentences.en: But anyway, I was about to say, Wilfred Owen, I did that at GCSE.
sentences.zh: 但不管怎样，我正要说的是，威尔弗雷德·欧文，我当年在GCSE（普通中等教育证书）考试时学过这个。

sentences.en: And pretty much exactly that moment, Blackadder Goes Forth, was going out on whatever it was, BBC One.
sentences.zh: 几乎就在那个时候，《黑爵士第四季》正在BBC One或其他什么频道热播。

sentences.en: So I was, as a teenager, completely steeped in that idea of the Western Front as this – a senseless waste.
sentences.zh: 所以作为一个青少年，我完全沉浸在那种将西线视为毫无意义的浪费的观念中——

sentences.en: I mean, that's the classic things that people say about it.
sentences.zh: 我的意思是，那是人们对此的经典评价。

sentences.en: War, what is it good for?
sentences.zh: 战争，究竟有何用处？

sentences.en: Yeah, precisely.
sentences.zh: 对，确切地说。

sentences.en: And actually, it was quite invigorating later on to start reading these books that said, actually, no, no, it was not a senseless waste.
sentences.zh: 事实上，后来开始阅读这些指出“其实并非如此，那并非毫无意义的浪费”的书籍，让人感到相当振奋。

sentences.en: A lot of people on the Western Front actually enjoyed it.
sentences.zh: 西线上的许多人其实还挺享受的。

sentences.en: The generals were much more canny than posterity kind of allows.
sentences.zh: 将军们比后人所认为的要精明得多。

sentences.en: And as it happens, we've got one of the absolute kind of key figures in that argument, Professor Gary Sheffield.
sentences.zh: 而碰巧的是，我们请来了这一论点的绝对关键人物之一，加里·谢菲尔德教授。

sentences.en: Anyway, Tom, you've probably got a better introduction for him than I do.
sentences.zh: 总之，汤姆，你对他的介绍大概比我要好。

sentences.en: Well, no, absolutely.
sentences.zh: 哦，不，绝对没有。

sentences.en: I mean, Gary Sheffield is – I mean, he's completely transformed the understanding of the First World War.
sentences.zh: 我的意思是，加里·谢菲尔德——我是说，他彻底改变了人们对第一次世界大战的理解。

sentences.en: So really, there's no one better to have on the show to look at the history of the Western Front, but also the various ways in which it's been understood.
sentences.zh: 所以真的没有人比他更适合做客节目来探讨西线的历史，以及人们理解它的各种方式了。

sentences.en: And I guess, Gary, the book you asked me to mention before we started this podcast was Forgotten Victory, the First World War, Myths and Realities.
sentences.zh: 我想，加里，你在我们开始录播客之前让我提的那本书是《被遗忘的胜利：第一次世界大战的迷思与现实》。

sentences.en: So I guess we're going to be talking quite a lot about myths and realities in this show.
sentences.zh: 所以我想我们在这期节目里会深入探讨很多关于迷思与现实的话题。

sentences.en: I think the title gives a little clue to my views, yes.
sentences.zh: 我想书名已经对我的观点给出了少许暗示，是的。

sentences.en: OK, well, before we get on to the myths and realities, could you just give us a sense of why the Western Front comes into existence?
sentences.zh: 好的，那么在我们探讨迷思与现实之前，你能否跟我们讲讲西线战场究竟是如何形成的？

sentences.en: I mean, basically, it's because the war breaks out in the summer of 1914.
sentences.zh: 我的意思是，基本上是因为1914年夏天爆发了战争。

sentences.en: And to begin with, it's very mobile, isn't it?
sentences.zh: 而且一开始，战争是非常具有流动性的，对吧？

sentences.en: That's right.
sentences.zh: 没错。

sentences.en: Essentially, the Western Front comes into being because the German attempt to win the war very quickly in the West fails.
sentences.zh: 从根本上说，西线之所以形成，是因为德国在西方迅速赢得战争的企图失败了。

sentences.en: That the Germans, well, historians debate how close they came to defeating the Allied armies,
sentences.zh: 德国人——好吧，历史学家们一直在争论他们距离击败盟军究竟有多近，

sentences.en: primarily the French, because, of course, the British army at this stage is very small.
sentences.zh: 主要是法军，因为当然了，当时英国陆军的规模非常小。

sentences.en: And so, Gary, the measure of success for the Germans would have been to capture Paris.
sentences.zh: 所以，加里，对德国人来说，成功的标准就是攻占巴黎。

sentences.en: Is that basically...
sentences.zh: 基本上是这样……

sentences.en: That's what they were aiming to do.
sentences.zh: 这正是他们当时的目标。

sentences.en: Whether that actually would have knocked France out of the war is another matter.
sentences.zh: 至于这是否真的能把法国打出战争，则是另一回事了。

sentences.en: But they don't succeed in capturing Paris.
sentences.zh: 但他们并没有成功攻占巴黎。

sentences.en: And perhaps even more importantly, they don't succeed in inflicting a crippling blow on the French army.
sentences.zh: 也许更重要的是，他们没能对法军给予致命一击。

sentences.en: Basically, what the Germans are hoping to do in 1914 is to repeat 1870, when the German field armies defeated the French field armies in a matter of months.
sentences.zh: 基本上，德国人在1914年希望做的是复制1870年的一幕，当时德军野战部队在几个月内就击败了法军野战部队。

sentences.en: And that's for a whole range of reasons.
sentences.zh: 这背后有各种各样的原因。

sentences.en: That does not happen in 1914.
sentences.zh: 但这并没有在1914年发生。

sentences.en: Instead, what happens is that both sides stumble upon something they've really known about already.
sentences.zh: 相反，发生的情况是，交战双方都不约而同地采用了一种他们其实早已知晓的办法。

sentences.en: That is, that if you are about to be outflanked or defeated, you get your soldiers to dig holes in the ground, long, thin holes.
sentences.zh: 那就是，如果你即将被包抄或击败，你就会让士兵在地上挖洞，又长又细的洞。

sentences.en: You put your soldiers in them, in these trenches, and suddenly it becomes much more difficult to kill these soldiers.
sentences.zh: 你把士兵安置在这些战壕里，突然之间，要杀死这些士兵就变得困难得多了。

sentences.en: For the simple reason that if you put a man in a hole, give him a bit of head cover, put a bit of barbed wire out in front, he's actually quite a difficult target to hit.
sentences.zh: 原因很简单，如果你把一个人放进洞里，给他提供一点顶部掩护，在前方拉上一段铁丝网，他实际上就会成为一个非常难被击中的目标。

sentences.en: But the poor so-and-sos who have to advance across the open towards the trenches are, of course, much more vulnerable.
sentences.zh: 但那些不得不冒着开阔地向战壕推进的可怜虫们，当然就脆弱得多了。

sentences.en: And add to the fact that by 1914, weapons are extremely powerful.
sentences.zh: 再加上到1914年时，武器已经变得极其强大。

sentences.en: I mean, there's been a revolution in firepower over the last hundred years.
sentences.zh: 我的意思是，在过去的百年里，火力经历了一场革命。

sentences.en: Because don't forget, 99 years before the First World War breaks out is the Battle of Waterloo, in which you have armies basically standing up, you know,
sentences.zh: 因为别忘了，第一次世界大战爆发前99年是滑铁卢战役，当时的军队基本上是列队站立，你知道的，

sentences.en: a few yards from each other, blazing away.
sentences.zh: 彼此相距仅几码，猛烈开火。

sentences.en: By 1914, that is no longer possible because of the power of the weapons, the sheer size of the armies, which, you know,
sentences.zh: 到了1914年，由于武器的威力以及军队的庞大体量，这已经不再可能了。你知道的，

sentences.en: go from being perhaps 100,000 strong, thereabouts at Waterloo, to millions strong.
sentences.zh: 军队规模从滑铁卢时期的可能10万人左右，激增到数百万之众。

sentences.en: And all, of course, these are major industrial powers backed by vast economies, which become even more powerful as they are developed to support the war effort.
sentences.zh: 当然，所有这些都是由庞大经济体支撑的主要工业强国，随着它们为支持战争努力而不断发展，其力量变得更加强大。

sentences.en: Cut a long story short, all this means is that the armies are unable to break the deadlock, which comes into being by the middle of November 1914.
sentences.zh: 长话短说，这一切意味着，军队无法打破在1914年11月中旬形成的僵局。

sentences.en: And it's in place largely, although not entirely, until the spring of 1918.
sentences.zh: 而且它在很大程度上——尽管并非全部——一直维持到1918年春季。

sentences.en: And in big handfuls, it's easy to explain in, it's fairly easy to explain in technical terms why.
sentences.zh: 简单概括一下，从技术层面解释原因其实并不算太难。

sentences.en: It's that the defender, having these mans in a hole already mentioned, can bring a vast amount of firepower to bear.
sentences.zh: 原因在于，正如刚才提到的，防守方让士兵呆在洞里，能够集中极其强大的火力。

sentences.en: And also that when an attacker breaks into an enemy position,
sentences.zh: 而且当进攻方突入敌方阵地时，

sentences.en: normally they are so weakened by the effort that they simply don't have enough men to throw through to exploit the gap that's made.
sentences.zh: 通常他们由于精疲力竭而极度虚弱，根本没有足够的人员投入来扩大已经打开的缺口。

sentences.en: And also because they lack communications in the way that they would have in the Second World War by radio,
sentences.zh: 而且由于他们不像第二次世界大战那样拥有无线电通讯，

sentences.en: or they lack the ability to pass messages by courier or rider or something, as had been the case perhaps even 50 or 60 years before,
sentences.zh: 或者他们缺乏像五六十年前那样通过信使、骑兵或其他方式传递信息的能力，

sentences.en: because armies are so big and so dispersed that they simply can't sum up reserves at the right place at the right time.
sentences.zh: 因为军队规模太庞大、太分散，以至于根本无法在正确的时间、正确的地点调集预备队。

sentences.en: Of course, the defender, who is dug in, has telephone wires buried deep beneath the ground,
sentences.zh: 当然，已经构筑好工事的防御方，地下埋有纵横交错的电话线，

sentences.en: and he could actually get a message back and rush people up to the right place at the right time.
sentences.zh: 他们实际上可以把消息传回后方，并在正确的时间将部队迅速调遣到正确的地点。

sentences.en: And what happens is, over the next four years, that the armies on the Western Front, the French, the Germans, the British,
sentences.zh: 于是发生的情况是，在接下来的四年里，西线战场上的法军、德军、英军，

sentences.en: struggle with coming up with technological ways of breaking this deadlock.
sentences.zh: 都在艰难地寻找打破这种僵局的技术手段。

sentences.en: In the end, they do, but it's enormously bloody.
sentences.zh: 最终他们做到了，但代价是极其血腥的。

sentences.en: And, in a sense, the answer to the question, why the casualties are so heavy, is that if you fight that sort of war, that are the sorts of casualties you end up with.
sentences.zh: 从某种意义上说，对“为什么伤亡如此惨重”这一问题的回答是：如果你打那种类型的战争，你最终就会承受那种类型的伤亡。

sentences.en: And really, the failure to come up with some sort of compromise peace, which is a political, not a military decision, condemns the armies to fight those sorts of battles.
sentences.zh: 说到底，未能达成某种妥协性的和平——这是一个政治决定，而非军事决定——注定了军队只能去打那种类型的战役。

sentences.en: Now, you can argue about the competence of generals and competence of individual armies,
sentences.zh: 现在，你可以争论将军们的指挥能力以及各个军队的作战素养，

sentences.en: but they're the fundamental reasons why the Western Front turns out to be as stalemated and as bloody as it is.
sentences.zh: 但这些才是西线战场最终陷入僵局且如此血腥的根本原因。

sentences.en: So, if we go back to the autumn of 1914, so the Germans have been pushed back from Paris at the Battle of the Marne.
sentences.zh: 所以，如果我们回到1914年秋天，德国人在马恩河战役中被从巴黎击退。

sentences.en: They've ended up on these, they have a race to the sea, don't they, where they try to outflank each other, and they end up with these lines etched into the map of Europe.
sentences.zh: 他们最终来到了这些地方，他们进行了一场“奔向大海”的竞赛，对吧？他们试图迂回包抄对方，最后在欧洲地图上留下了这些深深镌刻的战线。

sentences.en: And is this, so they tell the soldiers to dig, and they dig the trenches.
sentences.zh: 那么，这就是——他们命令士兵挖掘，于是士兵们挖了战壕。

sentences.en: Now, is this something that people, there was a revelation to them?
sentences.zh: 这在当时对人们来说，是一个全新的启示吗？

sentences.en: I mean, so Dave Walters, who's a regular listener to The Rest is History, has said, you know, did each side expect the war to be so static?
sentences.zh: 我的意思是，作为《历史的剩余部分》的常听众，戴夫·沃尔特斯曾说过，你知道的，交战双方是否都预料到战争会如此陷入僵局？

sentences.en: So, they have the technology.
sentences.zh: 所以，他们拥有相关技术。

sentences.en: I mean, they know that both sides have got machine guns, they know they've all got barbed wire and all these things.
sentences.zh: 我的意思是，他们知道双方都有机枪，知道大家都有铁丝网以及所有这些东西。

sentences.en: But is this a great shock to them, the generals and the soldiers?
sentences.zh: 但这对于将军们和战壕里的士兵来说，是一个巨大的震撼吗？

sentences.en: Yeah, it's putting it too strongly to say it's a shock, but it certainly comes with an unpleasant surprise,
sentences.zh: 是的，如果说这是个“震撼”就有点言过其实了，但它确实伴随着一个不愉快的惊喜，

sentences.en: because they are well aware that conflicts of this sort can be stalemated.
sentences.zh: 因为他们非常清楚，这种冲突可能会陷入僵局。

sentences.en: Only 10 years before, the Russo-Japanese War had seen a sort of Western Front-style conflict in Manchuria.
sentences.zh: 就在仅仅10年前，日俄战争就在满洲见证了一种西线风格的冲突。

sentences.en: And so you had trenches, you had stalemate all the rest of it.
sentences.zh: 所以当时有战壕，有僵局，诸如此类。

sentences.en: The thing is, this was broken after about nine months, a year, for a whole host of reasons that was not possible on the Western Front.
sentences.zh: 问题是，由于种种在西线无法复制的原因，这种情况在大约九个月到一年后就被打破了。

sentences.en: So, nobody really thought it would happen in the West, but they weren't entirely surprised when it did.
sentences.zh: 因此，没有人真正认为这会在西方发生，但当它真的发生时，他们也并不是完全感到意外。

sentences.en: Right.
sentences.zh: 没错。

sentences.en: I should actually say that the lessons of recent wars are always ambiguous.
sentences.zh: 我其实应该说，近期战争的经验教训总是模棱两可的。

sentences.en: And you had the British, actually, the most recent example of modern warfare was the Second Boer War in South Africa, 1899 to 1902.
sentences.zh: 而英国人——事实上，最近的一次现代战争范例是1899年至1902年在南非爆发的第二次布尔战争。

sentences.en: And the lessons from that war were rather different from those of Manchuria.
sentences.zh: 那场战争得出的教训与满洲之战相当不同。

sentences.en: And so people came into wars not necessarily having drawn the wrong lessons from history, but have not necessarily got all the lessons in the right balance.
sentences.zh: 因此，人们参战时，未必是从历史中汲取了错误的教训，而是未能将所有的教训完美地平衡好。

sentences.en: So, right at the beginning of the First World War, people still have a lot of faith in cavalry, don't they?
sentences.zh: 所以，就在第一次世界大战刚爆发时，人们对骑兵仍然抱有很大的信心，对吧？

sentences.en: So, the French go famously riding in coloured uniforms and nice helmets and swords and all that sort of stuff.
sentences.zh: 因此，法军出名地穿着色彩鲜艳的制服、戴着漂亮的头盔、挥舞着战刀等等诸如此类地骑马冲锋。

sentences.en: And Douglas Haig, of course, is a great cavalryman, isn't he?
sentences.zh: 而道格拉斯·黑格，当然也是一位伟大的骑兵将领，对吗？

sentences.en: Uh, he is and he isn't.
sentences.zh: 呃，他既是也不是。

sentences.en: Now, why I say that is if you, if by a traditional cavalryman, you know, with lots of waving swords and what have you, no, he isn't.
sentences.zh: 我之所以这么说是因为，如果你所指的是那种挥舞着马刀之类的传统骑兵，不，他不是。

sentences.en: Because cavalry, as far as the likes of Haig and the reformer school are concerned by this stage, has reinvented itself as effectively a new form of, as a new arm of warfare.
sentences.zh: 因为在黑格和改革派看来，到了这个阶段，骑兵已经自我重塑，实际上成了战争中的一个新兵种、一种新的作战力量。

sentences.en: Because cavalry in 1914, British cavalry anyway, they walk as much as they ride.
sentences.zh: 因为在1914年，英国骑兵——无论如何——步行的距离和他们骑马的距离差不多。

sentences.en: They are very well trained in firearMs.
sentences.zh: 他们在火器使用方面受过极佳的训练。

sentences.en: They have machine guns.
sentences.zh: 他们配备有机枪。

sentences.en: They have light artillery with them.
sentences.zh: 他们随身携带轻型火炮。

sentences.en: And the idea is that they will form effectively a sort of mobile column, which we see much use in the Second World War and beyond.
sentences.zh: 其理念是，他们将有效地组成某种机动纵队，我们在第二次世界大战及以后看到了这种战术的大量应用。

sentences.en: The difference is, of course, you're actually using horse flesh rather than vehicle.
sentences.zh: 当然，不同之处在于，你实际上使用的是马匹而非车辆。

sentences.en: So, yes, Haig does believe in charging forward, the arm blanche, if the moment is right.
sentences.zh: 所以，是的，如果时机成熟的话，黑格确实相信发起冲锋——也就是冷兵器冲锋（l'arme blanche）。

sentences.en: Actually, these moments actually do occur during the war, but it's not traditional cavalry.
sentences.zh: 事实上，战争期间确实出现了这样的时刻，但那已经不是传统骑兵了。

sentences.en: And interestingly, in 1914, the British cavalry is much better at doing the job of recce scouting
sentences.zh: 有趣的是，在1914年，英国骑兵在执行侦察和掩护撤退任务方面，

sentences.en: and covering the retreat than the French and the Germans, who are still much more wedded to traditional forms of cavalry.
sentences.zh: 比法军和德军要出色得多，后两者依然更加拘泥于传统的骑兵形式。

sentences.en: So I know it sort of sounds heretical to say it, but in the British army, the cavalry is some of the most advanced troops that Britain has in 1914.
sentences.zh: 所以我知道这样说听起来有点离经叛道，但在1914年的英国陆军中，骑兵其实是英国拥有的最先进的部队之一。

sentences.en: And so when do the generals and when do the troops in the trenches begin to realise
sentences.zh: 那么，将军们和战壕里的士兵究竟是在什么时候开始意识到

sentences.en: the nature of the war that they're involved in?
sentences.zh: 他们所卷入的这场战争的本质的呢？

sentences.en: Well, in one sense, very early on, because casualties are staggeringly high from the beginning.
sentences.zh: 嗯，从某种意义上说，非常早，因为伤亡人数从一开始就高得惊人。

sentences.en: Much higher than they had experienced in the Boer War, and in fact, much higher than the planning for replacing troops
sentences.zh: 远高于他们在布尔战争中经历过的水平，事实上，也远高于战前在补充部队规划

sentences.en: and indeed for replenishing stocks of shells before the war had taken on board.
sentences.zh: 以及补充炮弹库存方面所做准备的预期。

sentences.en: So no one is in any illusion at all by about September, October, November 1914.
sentences.zh: 所以在1914年的9月、10月、11月左右，已经没有人再抱有任何幻想了。

sentences.en: This is a very bloody war.
sentences.zh: 这是一场非常血腥的战争。

sentences.en: Gary, had anyone actually said it will be over by Christmas, or is that a myth?
sentences.zh: 加里，真的有人说过“圣诞节前就能结束”吗，还是这只个传说？

sentences.en: Well, various people did say that, but it certainly wasn't a sort of planning assumption of the army.
sentences.zh: 嗯，确实有不同的人说过这话，但这绝对不是军队的某种作战规划假设。

sentences.en: After all, because when Kitchener becomes Secretary of State for War in August 1914, he immediately announces this war is going to last at least three years.
sentences.zh: 毕竟，当基钦纳于1914年8月担任陆军大臣时，他立即宣布这场战争将持续至少三年。

sentences.en: Yeah, and the Germans too.
sentences.zh: 对，德国人也是如此。

sentences.en: I mean, the Germans, there's lots of quotes, aren't there, from Moltke and the other generals who sort of say, well, we hope we're going to win it quickly,
sentences.zh: 我的意思是，德国人那边有很多名言，对吧？来自毛奇和其他将领，他们大意是说，嗯，我们希望能够快速赢得战争，

sentences.en: but if we don't, it's going to be an absolute nightmare and all Europe will be consumed and all this.
sentences.zh: 但如果我们做不到，那将是一场绝对的噩梦，整个欧洲都将被吞噬，诸如此类。

sentences.en: Well, in fact, it's Moltke the Elder who famously says something about, I think, in the 1890s at the end of his life.
sentences.zh: 嗯，事实上，老毛奇在1890年代他生命快结束时，曾就此发表过一些著名的言论。

sentences.en: So the Germans actually come into the war really staking everything on a quick win, and when it doesn't happen, they think, well, what are we going to do now?
sentences.zh: 所以德国人参战时确实把一切都押在了速战速决上，当这没有发生时，他们想，好吧，我们现在该怎么办？

sentences.en: And they then have to improvise a prolonged form of warfare, which, of course, they do up to a point quite successfully, after they keep the war going for another four years.
sentences.zh: 于是他们不得不即兴进行一场长期的战争，当然，他们在某种程度上做得相当成功，他们让战争又持续了四年。

sentences.en: But there's no attempt at this, when they start to realise that it's going to be a deadlock,
sentences.zh: 但当他们开始意识到这是一场僵局、一场极其血腥的僵局时，难道就没有人试图达成某种和平吗？

sentences.en: a horribly bloody deadlock, there's no attempt to kind of arrive at a peace?
sentences.zh: 呃，在整个战争期间，零星出现过达成和平条款的尝试。

sentences.en: Well, there are sporadic attempts to come to peace terms throughout the war.
sentences.zh: 事实上，我马上就要暴露自己的彻底无知了，我要说的是，最近刚出版了一本书，

sentences.en: In fact, I'm about to reveal my complete numptiness by saying a book has been published very recently, arguing there were some very serious attempts to negotiate peace in 1950,
sentences.zh: 声称在1915年、1916年有一些非常严肃的谈判和平的尝试。
我不记得作者的名字了，而且我也没有读过这本书，所以除此之外，我无法提供更多信息。

sentences.en: I can't remember the name of the author, and I haven't read the book, so beyond that, I can't point.
sentences.zh: 欢迎来到我们的播客。

sentences.en: Welcome to our podcaSt.
sentences.zh: 我听过你们的很多播客节目。

sentences.en: I've listened to many of your podcasts.
sentences.zh: 我只想说，我对这件事的看法是，很难看出西方怎么可能会出现妥协性的和平，因为这需要德国人做出妥协，而就目前而言……

sentences.en: All I would say is that my take on it is, it's difficult to see how there could be a compromise peace in the West, because it would involve the Germans compromising, and as far
sentences.zh: 这需要德国人做出妥协，而就目前而言……

sentences.en: as I can see, they were never prepared to abandon territory in the West, even though it clearly would have been of their advantage to do so.
sentences.zh: 在我看来，他们从来没有准备好放弃西线领土，尽管这样做显然对他们有利。

sentences.en: So, for example, at the end of 1917, when they have knocked, effectively they've knocked
sentences.zh: 所以，举个例子，在1917年底，当他们实际上已经把

sentences.en: Russia off the war, the Germans win the First World War Part One, which is against Russia.
sentences.zh: 俄国打出了一战的第一部分，也就是对俄作战。

sentences.en: At that point, had they sort of moved from the battlefield to the negotiating table, I'm pretty
sentences.zh: 在那个时候，如果他们从战场转向谈判桌，我相当

sentences.en: sure they could have come up with a very favourable peace, as in give back all the stuff they conquered in the West, and you've still won.
sentences.zh: 确信他们本可以达成一项非常有利的和平协议，比如归还他们在西线征服的所有土地，而你依然赢了。

sentences.en: You've got all of the Russian Empire to exploit and to build upon.
sentences.zh: 你拥有整个俄罗斯帝国可以开发和建设。

sentences.en: The Germans choose not to do that.
sentences.zh: 德国人选择不这样做。

sentences.en: They decide they're going to go for broke by attacking in the West, and of course, in the end, that actually brings them down.
sentences.zh: 他们决定在西线发起进攻，孤注一掷，当然，到头来，这实际上导致了他们的垮台。

sentences.en: So, I haven't read the book, so I can't comment on the argument, but actually, from my reading
sentences.zh: 所以，我没读过这本书，所以我无法对这个观点发表评论，但实际上，从我对

sentences.en: of the evidence, there's very little scope for compromise, because the Germans are simply not prepared to make those compromises.
sentences.zh: 证据的阅读来看，妥协的余地非常小，因为德国人根本不准备做出那些妥协。

sentences.en: And afterwards, the French have got the Germans sitting on their territory, why should they compromise?
sentences.zh: 而且后来，法国人看到德国人占据了他们的领土，他们为什么要妥协？

sentences.en: Yeah, yeah.
sentences.zh: 对，对。

sentences.en: And also, Tom, I was thinking about this today, because I knew this would come up.
sentences.zh: 而且，汤姆，我今天也在想这件事，因为我知道这会被问到。

sentences.en: It's a bit like our Vietnam podcast that we did with Andrea Preston, about why the Americans kept on with the commitment.
sentences.zh: 这有点像我们和安德烈·普雷斯顿一起做的关于越战的播客，关于为什么美国人会坚持到底。

sentences.en: I mean, politically, I think with wars, when you go in, you go all in, and you sort of say, well, this is essential for our national honour and for our national survival.
sentences.zh: 我的意思是，在政治上，我认为对于战争，一旦你介入，你就会全力以赴，然后你会说，嗯，这对于我们的国家荣誉和国家生存至关重要。

sentences.en: And it becomes very difficult then, after a year or two years, to say, you know what, actually, it's not really essential.
sentences.zh: 然后在一年或两年后，你就会发现，很难再开口说，你知道吗，实际上，这其实并非必不可少。

sentences.en: We can just do a deal.
sentences.zh: 我们完全可以做个交易。

sentences.en: I mean, well, not least because you're betraying, you're effectively betraying everybody who's
sentences.zh: 我的意思是，最起码因为你在背叛，你实际上是在背叛所有

sentences.en: already died, and all the bereaved, to whom you have said it was absolutely essential that they died, and we are now committed to winning the war.
sentences.zh: 已经死去的人，以及所有失去亲属的人——你曾向他们信誓旦旦地说，他们的死绝对至关重要，而我们现在致力于赢得这场战争。

sentences.en: And actually, Gary will know this much better than me, if you read what the soldiers themselves
sentences.zh: 实际上，加里对这方面的了解比我多得多，如果你读读士兵们自己的

sentences.en: were saying, like the British soldiers, for example, they would often say, well, I'm determined, you know, we have to finish the job.
sentences.zh: 言论，比如英国士兵，他们经常会说，嗯，我下定决心了，你知道的，我们必须完成任务。

sentences.en: We're in this for a reason.
sentences.zh: 我们卷入这场战争是有原因的。

sentences.en: You know, lots of them were very patriotic, and they wanted to win.
sentences.zh: 你知道，他们当中很多人都极具爱国热情，并且渴望胜利。

sentences.en: Absolutely.
sentences.zh: 完全正确。

sentences.en: If I could chuck in the name of a book I can remember the title of, by my friend, Mike
sentences.zh: 如果我可以插播一本我还记得书名的书，作者是我朋友

sentences.en: Nyberg, a very distinguished American historian of the First World War, Dance of the Furies.
sentences.zh: 迈克·尼伯格，一位非常杰出的美国第一次世界大战历史学家，书名叫《复仇之舞》。

sentences.en: He argues that actually, there wasn't a great deal of hatred which propelled the peoples of Europe into war in August 1914.
sentences.zh: 他认为，实际上，在1914年8月，并没有多少仇恨推动欧洲人民走向战争。

sentences.en: But after war broke out, yes, that hatred did pile up, not least because of the vast losses.
sentences.zh: 但战争爆发后，是的，这种仇恨确实积聚起来了，这很大程度上是因为巨大的伤亡。

sentences.en: And it becomes, you know, are you going to betray the people who've died already by making a compromised peace?
sentences.zh: 于是这就变成了，你知道的，你难道要通过缔结妥协的和平来背叛那些已经牺牲的人吗？

sentences.en: And where is the hatred most visceral?
sentences.zh: 哪里的仇恨最撕心裂肺？

sentences.en: In the trenches or back home?
sentences.zh: 是在战壕里，还是在后方？

sentences.en: It tends to be on the home fronts, actually.
sentences.zh: 实际上，往往是在大后方。

sentences.en: There's a sort of a bit of a sort of sentimental idea that all the men in the trenches admired each other.
sentences.zh: 有一种略带感伤的想法，认为战壕里所有的人都互相钦佩。

sentences.en: They were all fellow sufferers.
sentences.zh: 他们都是同甘共苦的难兄难弟。

sentences.en: There's certainly a bit of that.
sentences.zh: 这当中确实有一点这种成分。

sentences.en: There's also a lot of, I think, individual hatred of shooting prisoners out of hand, of failing to take prisoners in the first place.
sentences.zh: 但我认为，其中也包含很多个人的仇恨，比如随手枪杀战俘，或者一开始就根本不接受战俘。

sentences.en: I wouldn't overstress it, but it does tend to be on the home front that you get, you know, the real demagogues in Britain, France, Germany, and elsewhere kicking up this fuss.
sentences.zh: 我不想过分夸大这一点，但在英国、法国、德国及其他地方煽动这种喧嚣的，往往确实是大后方的那些真正的蛊惑者。

sentences.en: But it does feed into a total war mentality.
sentences.zh: 但这确实助长了一种全面战争的心态。

sentences.en: And once you have turned that on, it is very difficult to turn it off again.
sentences.zh: 一旦你开启了这种心态，想要再关掉它就极其困难了。

sentences.en: Right.
sentences.zh: 没错。

sentences.en: So on the topic of the experience of the soldiers in the trenches, we had loads of questions about this.
sentences.zh: 所以在关于战壕中士兵经历这个话题上，我们收到了大量相关的问题。

sentences.en: And we began with Wilfred Owen.
sentences.zh: 我们从威尔弗雷德·欧文谈起。

sentences.en: And that's the kind of conventional sense is that it's all slaughter, blood, horror, rats, gangrene, whatever.
sentences.zh: 传统观念通常认为，战争就是屠杀、鲜血、恐怖、老鼠、坏疽，诸如此类。

sentences.en: But we've got a question from Mark Brooks.
sentences.zh: 但我们收到了马克·布鲁克斯的一个问题。

sentences.en: What do you think of the view proposed by Neil Ferguson that many soldiers actually enjoyed their war term experience?
sentences.zh: 你如何看待尼尔·弗格森提出的观点，即许多士兵其实很享受他们的战争经历？

sentences.en: And from Bariga or Barija, many historians who interviewed
sentences.zh: 还有来自巴里加或巴里加的问题，许多采访过

sentences.en: First World War, infantry veterans say the survivors never talk of the horrors of the trenches, but more of mateship and comradeship.
sentences.zh: 第一次世界大战步兵老兵的历史学家说，幸存者从不谈论战壕的恐怖，更多谈到的是战友情谊。

sentences.en: Yeah.
sentences.zh: 是的。

sentences.en: You know, was war hell or was it actually, did people enjoy it?
sentences.zh: 你知道，战争到底是人间地狱，还是说其实人们挺享受的？

sentences.en: I think a very few people actually enjoyed the war in a sense they liked the killing and the violence.
sentences.zh: 我认为极少数人真正享受战争，在这个意义上他们喜欢杀戮和暴力。

sentences.en: Hitler, of course, famous example of that.
sentences.zh: 希特勒当然就是一个著名的例子。

sentences.en: Ernst Jünger, Storm of Steel, all the rest of it.
sentences.zh: 恩斯特·容格的《钢铁风暴》等等。

sentences.en: And they're British equivalents.
sentences.zh: 还有他们的英国同行。

sentences.en: I mean, interestingly, Siegfried Sassoon was known as Mad Jack within the regiment because he was a suicidally brave officer.
sentences.zh: 有趣的是，西格弗里德·萨松在团里被称为“疯子杰克”，因为他是一个敢于拼命的勇敢军官。

sentences.en: So you could actually have very ambiguous views about the war.
sentences.zh: 所以你实际上可以对战争持有非常矛盾的看法。

sentences.en: You could actually enjoy it and still, you know, hate it in other ways.
sentences.zh: 你一方面可以享受它，但同时（你知道的）在其他方面又痛恨它。

sentences.en: In a broader sense, I think many men did, again, enjoy putting it too strongly, but actually they didn't mind the war, at least military experience.
sentences.zh: 从更广泛的意义上讲，我认为许多人确实——同样，这样说可能有些过分，但实际上他们并不介意战争，至少不介意军事经历。

sentences.en: And all sorts of reasons for this.
sentences.zh: 原因有很多种。

sentences.en: If you are poor on the margins of society, the army will feed you three times a day and give you a stout pair of boots.
sentences.zh: 如果你是一个处于社会边缘的穷人，军队一天会喂你三顿饭，还发给你一双结实的靴子。

sentences.en: It comes up at that sort of simple level.
sentences.zh: 问题就落在这个相对简单的层面。

sentences.en: If you are a city clerk, an incredibly boring job in London, you suddenly are out of the fresh air, training with your mates and all the rest of it.
sentences.zh: 如果你是一个城市职员，在伦敦做着一份极其无聊的工作，你突然呼吸到了新鲜空气，和战友们一起训练，诸如此类。

sentences.en: Of course, once you get to the Western Front, it's different and all the rest of it.
sentences.zh: 当然，一旦你到了西线，情况就完全不同了，诸如此类。

sentences.en: But people do have very mixed and ambiguous responses to the war.
sentences.zh: 但人们对战争确实有着非常复杂和矛盾的反应。

sentences.en: I actually interviewed a few Great War veterans.
sentences.zh: 我实际上采访过几位第一次世界大战的老兵。

sentences.en: I was in my twenties in the early eighties doing post-grad degrees.
sentences.zh: 我在八十年代初二十多岁的时候正在读研究生学位。

sentences.en: And I didn't find any of them who really said, oh, the war was terrible.
sentences.zh: 我没有发现他们当中有谁真的说，哦，战争太可怕了。

sentences.en: Everybody hated it.
sentences.zh: 每个人都痛恨它。

sentences.en: Many of them had a much more nuanced view.
sentences.zh: 他们中的许多人有着更加微妙的看法。

sentences.en: Quite a number actually dismissed what we would now call the Blackadder view, of course, is slightly before Blackadder, as simply, well,
sentences.zh: 相当一部分人实际上驳斥了我们现在所说的“黑爵士”观点——当然，这比《黑爵士》出现的时间要稍微早一点——他们认为这很简单，就是

sentences.en: you know, okay, it's a bit of knockabout fun.
sentences.zh: 你知道的，好吧，这不过是一场打闹游戏罢了。

sentences.en: And in the same way, various work has been done on veterans who saw, oh, what a lovely war, both the play and the film in the 1960s.
sentences.zh: 同样，人们也对那些看过《多可爱的战争》的老兵做过各种研究，无论是1960年代的戏剧还是电影。

sentences.en: And some of them really enjoyed it because they're actually singing the songs of the trenches they remembered, but they rejected the overall message.
sentences.zh: 其中有些人真的很喜欢，因为他们实际上在唱着他们记忆中的战壕歌曲，但他们拒绝接受其整体传达的信息。

sentences.en: Yeah, I've heard that story.
sentences.zh: 对，我听说过这个故事。

sentences.en: Isn't there a story about a group of veterans who go on a trip to see the play or something?
sentences.zh: 是不是有个故事说，有一群老兵去旅行看话剧还是别的什么？

sentences.en: And at the interval, they're all kind of singing the songs and they're chatting, oh, do you remember when that bloke had his head blown off?
sentences.zh: 然后在幕间休息时，他们都在那儿唱着歌聊天，哦，你还记得当年哪个家伙脑袋被炸飞了吗？

sentences.en: Or it's kind of these sort of anecdotes, which in a way is not altogether surprising, is it?
sentences.zh: 或者类似这样的轶事，从某种程度上讲，其实也并不完全让人意外，对吧？

sentences.en: Because am I not right in thinking that if you're on the Western Front, if you're, certainly
sentences.zh: 因为我没记错的话，如果你身处西线，如果你是——当然

sentences.en: if you're a British soldier, you don't actually spend that much time in the trench at the front.
sentences.zh: 如果你是一个英国士兵，你其实并不会在最前线的战壕里花太多时间。

sentences.en: You spend a lot of time behind the trenches, don't you?
sentences.zh: 你花很多时间在战壕后面，对吧？

sentences.en: Absolutely, you do.
sentences.zh: 完全正确，确实如此。

sentences.en: The idea that soldiers sort of arrived in France in August 1914 and stood up to their waists in mud until November 1918 is simply untrue.
